US Intelligence Hawks Plot to Sneak Through Warrantless Spying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:29:16 UTC
01:29:16 KST

This article was featured in the Daily Prospect newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Intelligence hawks are once again posturing to help the Trump administration reauthorize its warrantless surveillance program, even as the outlook for privacy reforms has been boosted considerably by midterm victories in the House and Senate. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politico the strategy: reauthorize Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), which expired in June, by attaching it to the typically must-pass National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) before the lame-duck session comes to an end.
Democratic intelligence hawks have kept their cards close on whether they would support using the NDAA as a vehicle to renew the surveillance authority in the lame duck, but history suggests those hawks would be hard-pressed to miss the opportunity. In fact, Democratic supporters of Section 702 see the midterm triumph for their party as a bad development for their priorities.
Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), currently ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and the intelligence community’s strongest ally in Congress, knows that a clean reauthorization of Section 702 would be unlikely to pass after the lame-duck session. Himes, who is in line to chair the Intelligence Committee next year, told The Hill as much in an interview last week, arguing that Congress needs to “get this thing done in the lame duck because … it’s going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”
The Prospect in your inbox
Analysis that goes beyond the noise with in-depth, progressive reporting.
No paywall, no programmatic ads — just the reporting. Unsubscribe anytime. Submitting your email signs you up for The Daily Prospect, our weekday morning newsletter.
Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA), vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) have also backed a lame-duck FISA extension. (Kelly also serves on the Senate Intelligence Committee.)
According to Elizabeth Goitein, co-director of the Liberty and National Security Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, Himes and other Democratic intelligence hawks “are out of step with the rest of their caucus, and with the rest of Congress.” As the Prospect reported earlier this year, reclaiming the majority is one way to force fair votes on privacy reform, namely warrant requirements for any spying on Americans. “I don’t see a world in which Democratic leaders do not allow votes on reforms, no matter who the Democratic leaders are [in the next Congress],” Goitein said.
That’s why Democrats like Himes and Warner want to get Section 702 through now. But the opposition to a clean extension has proven to be increasingly transpartisan. And privacy advocates across the country and on Capitol Hill are gearing up for a year-end fight to stop the warrantless spying agenda in its tracks.
“Using must-pass legislation like the NDAA to yet again try to force a clean reauthorization of this powerful tool is a desperate move to advance a warrantless surveillance agenda that has been rejected by the majority of Americans,” Amanda Beckham, government relations director at Free Press Action, said in a statement.
FREE PRESS ACTION IS PART of a coalition of several dozen civil society groups seeking to thwart intelligence hawks’ efforts to extend Section 702 in the lame-duck session. That coalition, which includes Demand Progress, the Brennan Center for Justice, and many more, warned against renewing the government’s surveillance authority in letters to congressional leadership last week.
Currently, the NDAA is in a House-Senate conference committee, even though Democrats blocked a floor vote in the Senate in July. Negotiators are getting pressure from intelligence hawks to add FISA Section 702 to the final conference report, which should emerge in the coming weeks.
“Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process,” coalition member organizations wrote in a November 12 letter. The following day, they sent a second letter, this time to Democratic leadership. Mother Jones was the first to report that in it, the coalition laid out an anti-surveillance agenda for Democrats to prioritize in the next Congress, calling on them to “make protecting Americans’ privacy and reining in surveillance an urgent congressional priority.”
The NDAA has passed every year since 1961, an unparalleled streak for a Congress that doesn’t get much of anything done on time. My colleague Robert Kuttner observed earlier this month, however, that there has been “more than trivial Republican opposition” to this year’s NDAA. Some Democrats want to remove a provision that they say would intertwine the U.S. and Israeli militaries, while the $1.5 trillion price tag President Trump has set has brought opposition. Yet the NDAA always manages to pass, and usually other measures that members of Congress want to quietly advance hitch a ride on the defense bill.
If Himes is to be believed, Section 702 is the nation’s “most rigorously overseen” intelligence program, which he claims is not prone to abuse. Privacy advocates roll their eyes at that last line, as the FBI shuttered an office responsible for monitoring Section 702 abuses last year, and has been notoriously noncompliant with the existing yet limited guardrails for protecting Americans’ privacy.
While there is broad bipartisan support for reforms like warrant requirements, members of Congress had no opportunity to vote on those reforms this year. “The only reason we didn’t have votes in this Congress was because the Trump administration made sure of it, and Speaker Johnson was obviously carrying the administration’s water on that,” Goitein said. But Republicans could never get a majority for a clean reauthorization either, and the warrantless spying measure expired.
Republican opponents of privacy reform have begun to manufacture a false sense of urgency around Section 702. One particularly glaring example was the op-ed Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) co-authored for The Wall Street Journal last week, “A Vital National Security Tool Shouldn’t Go Dark.” Cornyn and his co-author, Strauss Center Director Adam Klein, argue that failing to renew Section 702 in the lame-duck session “is risky” because intelligence officials may not have enough time to “seek new court orders before the current ones expire.” The reality is that since the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) certified Section 702 through mid-March of next year, intelligence officials have ample time to file for new certifications.
“The moment that the government files an application for new certifications, that filing extends the existing certifications until the FISA court has the chance to rule,” Goitein said.
To avoid an actual lapse, the government would simply need to file an application before March 17, 2027, making that roughly the deadline for Congress to renew Section 702. Moreover, if the government does need more time, Congress can temporarily extend the existing certifications for a brief period.
The intelligence community itself has continued to deploy scare tactics in a bid to secure Congress’s blessing for a clean extension of the surveillance authority.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and CIA Director John Ratcliffe sent a letter to congressional leaders last week, warning that any delay in reauthorizing Section 702 would put “the lives of both Americans in the homeland and our troops stationed abroad at risk in the heightened threat environment.” They attributed that heightened threat environment to Iran, which intelligence officials reportedly claimed has plans to target senior members of the Trump administration, with either a dirty bomb or chemical weapons attack in Washington, D.C.
But some intelligence officials cast doubt on whether Iran could feasibly execute such a sophisticated act of terror in the U.S., and the White House asserted that at this time, “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Critics also drew comparisons between the alleged bomb plot and the U.S. invasion of Iraq.
HIMES TALKS A BIG GAME when it comes to his role in overseeing the intelligence community. Now that Democrats will enjoy majority control in both chambers come January, he’s been talking an even bigger one. Himes himself is expected to lead the House Intelligence Committee in the next Congress.
In an interview with The New York Times last week, Himes revealed plans to probe the expansion of the CIA’s “extremely aggressive” covert operations under the Trump administration, while opening investigations into defense and intelligence contractors over their donations to the president’s vanity projects.
But Democrats can do much more with their oversight power in the next Congress. The obvious start is to add warrant requirements to Section 702 as a condition for continuing the program. That is likely to have support from a bipartisan majority next year.
But more can be done. For instance, the Offices of the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) and U.S. Attorney General are required to submit semiannual reports to Congress on compliance with the statutory and constitutional requirements of Section 702.
“In the past, when these reports have been submitted,” Goitein said, “they’ve also been made public.”
The 29th Joint Assessment, which is the most recently declassified semiannual compliance report, was released in July 2025. According to an April 2026 staff report from the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board, the DNI and the attorney general have submitted Joint Assessments 30 through 33, none of which have been declassified. It also remains unclear whether the 34th and 35th Joint Assessments have been submitted by the DNI and the attorney general.
The Prospect in your inbox
Analysis that goes beyond the noise with in-depth, progressive reporting.
No paywall, no programmatic ads — just the reporting. Unsubscribe anytime. Submitting your email signs you up for The Daily Prospect, our weekday morning newsletter.
Another ripe area for intelligence community oversight in the next Congress is the failure of the DNI and the attorney general to declassify FISC’s March 2026 opinion by the statutory deadline on September 13. That opinion, in which the judge reportedly found serious issues with the filtering tools U.S. intelligence agencies use to sift through queries for information on individuals who have communicated with foreign intelligence targets, likely contains important information about how Section 702 is being run and could give a boost to reformers who want to fix the system. Sens. Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Adam Schiff (D-CA) have pressed the Trump administration for “flagrantly” violating the law.
What’s more, Wyden believes there are “credible allegations” that Clayton provided false testimony at his Senate confirmation hearing about the since-withdrawn subpoenas of New York Times journalists, which Clayton issued in the waning days of his tenure as the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
“I think more broadly across authorities,” said Goitein, “Congress should be looking into how the administration has used and abused its surveillance powers.”
Ramming through a clean extension of Section 702 in the lame duck would be an abdication of the duty Congress has to openly debate an issue as consequential as Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, privacy advocates say.
“If and when this gets brought to a vote in the next Congress, if Congressman Himes wants to make the case to his caucus for why Trump should have warrantless access to Americans’ communications, that’s his right,” Goitein told the Prospect. “Let’s have that debate.”

Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:28:12 UTC
01:28:12 KST

In 2015 Microsoft acquired a to-do list app called Wunderlist, for a price rumored to be as high as $200 million. Wunderlist fans were worried that Microsoft would make their beloved app soulless and corporate, or worse, hide it behind some convoluted enterprise subscription. But against all odds, Microsoft was a good steward: The app became Microsoft To Do, but it remained a useful and powerful way for people to manage their tasks across all platforms.
Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app
The Wunderlist era is officially over. Good luck getting your stuff out.
Now Microsoft is pulling the rug. Buried deep in a blog post about “unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365” is the news that the To Do apps will “retire” on June 30th, 2027. The transition will be painful: Starting next summer, business users will need to use the Planner app for their tasks, but Microsoft won’t migrate their tasks automatically. And personal users, well, don’t let the door hit you. “Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app,” the blog post reads.
From a certain strategic standpoint, you can almost see how this makes sense. (Microsoft hasn’t responded to a request for comment.) It’s definitely true that Microsoft’s task- and project-management offerings are too complicated; To Do and Planner have some overlapping features, and you can use a half-dozen different Microsoft apps to manage your daily tasks. Microsoft has been hinting at bringing everything under the Planner banner for some time, and as Microsoft tries to foist Copilot upon everything you do at work, bringing all that stuff into one place makes more sense.
(“More sense” may be relative, though. When your blog post contains sentences like, “Additionally, this unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier because it’s all part of Work IQ,” you still have some work to do.)
It’s also yet another sign that Microsoft is simply giving up on the idea of making software that people use outside of work. Planner isn’t available through a personal or family Microsoft 365 account, so you can’t switch if you want to. Not that you necessarily would: Lots of people liked To Do specifically because it was a list of tasks, not a project management platform. Planner is a business tool for business users, administered by IT professionals and monitored by big bosses.
Planner is also, in many ways, just not as good a platform. It doesn’t have a dedicated desktop app — you’re meant to use it on the web, or through Teams or Outlook — and is missing some of To Do’s useful syncing and sharing features. Microsoft is not promising to spend the next six months closing those gaps, or even offering to help people export their data and move on. The company is simply getting all the way out of the business of helping regular people manage their days, and leaving users in the lurch.
If you’re suddenly shopping for a new to-do list, the good news is there are plenty of good options. Todoist and TickTick are the two stalwarts of the space, and they offer much of the same ubiquity and simplicity as To Do (though I agree with all the commenters on Reddit and Microsoft’s blog, who say To Do’s interface was better than either one.) Google Tasks is being integrated across Google’s own office suite. The vibe coding revolution has also persuaded approximately every person on the internet to build their own to-do app, so you have lots to choose from. At this point, there’s seemingly only one company left that doesn’t want you managing your days and tasks in its systems, and it’s Microsoft.

ICE Is Paying AT&T to Dig Through a Mountain of Call Records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:24:31 UTC
01:24:31 KST

Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts have called it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data.
The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning non-customers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.
“This requirement provides ICE access to AT&T’s raw data and experienced analysts,” the document obtained by 404 Media reads.
AT&T told 404 Media the data is made available under a valid legal order, but experts point out it requires an administrative subpoena, which agencies can issue themselves and don’t require a judge’s approval, raising concerns that ICE can use the data for essentially whatever it wants. The document also shows how financial incentives play a part in providing data to ICE.
“The Biden administration shut down Hemisphere after I and Rep. Biggs repeatedly questioned this warrantless mass phone surveillance program. 404 Media’s reporting shows that the Trump-Vance administration has created a zombie version of Hemisphere surveillance, and given it to their chosen enforcers at ICE,” Senator Ron Wyden told 404 Media in a statement.
Christopher Soghoian, a surveillance expert who worked for Senator Wyden for a decade until September, told 404 Media, “It’s bad enough that AT&T is mining its customers’ private phone records as a paid service for ICE, but because AT&T is also mining the records of other wholesale telecom companies, consumers can’t vote with their wallets and switch carriers to protect their privacy.”
Last September, ICE posted a procurement record saying it awarded a contract to AT&T for access to its Data Analytics and Support Services. When ICE announced the purchase, an attached document to the listing was marked as “controlled” and not available to the public. 404 Media subsequently obtained the document through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with ICE. The Financial Times previously reported on the public procurement records but did not report on the restricted document at the time.
“OAQ [the Office of Acquisition Management] intends to procure, on a sole source basis, access to raw data and analytical services from a telecommunications company,” the restricted document reads. It says AT&T analysts will transform the AT&T data “into a suitable format” while “ensuring accurate technical interpretation to accomplish HSI’s investigative mission.” HSI is Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, which has traditionally focused on things like cybercrime and child abuse cases, but under the Trump administration has dramatically refocused on immigration violations and investigating voter fraud.
The document says the AT&T data will be used to support “a wide range of HSI investigations and agency priorities,” but the specific sorts of investigations, taking up several lines of the document, are redacted.
Another document previously obtained by Senator Wyden’s office lays out the sort of data collected by AT&T and the capabilities available under the Data Analytical Services program. Those services include linking multiple devices or phone numbers to an identified target; identifying devices that have had their SIM cards replaced; determining whether phones associated with an international investigation target have entered the U.S.; and deconflicting international phone numbers associated with targets. That document was provided by the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), an obscure White House-affiliated entity that previously funded the Hemisphere program, and which 404 Media reported is behind a growing nationwide network of automatic license plate readers (ALPRs). According to documents previously obtained by the EFF and EPIC, the AT&T program contains more than a trillion phone records.
Soghoian added AT&T also provides “wholesale service to other phone companies, helping them to deliver calls.” Through that, “AT&T is able to collect, save, and mine records of calls by customers of other companies, even conversations in which both callers use non-AT&T phone companies.”
The restricted document 404 Media obtained says that during Fiscal Year 2025, there was a higher demand for data provided by this AT&T system, and “further significant increase in use is anticipated.”
“AT&T is the only vendor who possesses the ability to access AT&T owned raw data,” the document continues. “The requirement is data and analytical services provided by AT&T. If AT&T does not execute the analytical work, the capability will be lost, as no other company has access to the data required.”
Public procurement records show ICE paid AT&T more than $2.1 million in 2025 for access to the service, and more than $2.2 million this August, with the possibility to pay up to more than ten million dollars over the coming years.
“ICE appears to have contracted for access to the same data and service AT&T provided for the Data Analytical Services (DAS) Program, formerly known as the Hemisphere Project, which is the largest telephone record collection program reported to date. ICE using DAS or something akin to it would potentially come with access to trillions of phone records and location data,” Jeramie Scott, senior counsel at EPIC and director of EPIC's Surveillance Oversight Program, told 404 Media. “This program is ripe for abuse and is being used by an agency known for the abuse of its authority.”
“This is AT&T continuing to leverage its phone service to conduct mass, indiscriminate surveillance to sell to law enforcement,” Scott added. “ICE is now taking advantage of AT&T’s surveillance as a service model while likely evading any judicial oversight and conducting no privacy impact assessment prior to using the service to determine whether it should be used in the first place. Spoiler alert: It shouldn’t!”
Scott pointed out the data likely includes location information too, and this raises the question whether the program violates the law given Supreme Court rulings Carpenter and Chatrie. The former ruled that law enforcement needed a warrant to obtain phone location data. The latter made a similar judgment around location data and geofence warrants.
“Americans are pushing back on government surveillance, from Flock cameras to FISA, all across the country and will be rightfully outraged that AT&T is allowing ICE to search through its customers' phone records without a warrant or court oversight,” Senator Wyden added.
An AT&T spokesperson told 404 Media in an email, “For decades, we have been a trusted partner to provide reliable connectivity to federal agencies as well as state and local governments. We are required by law to provide information to government and law enforcement agencies when it is demanded under lawful order. We ensure that these requests are valid, and that our responses comply with the law.”
After publication of this piece, AT&T provided a second statement: “The contract referenced is with the Department of Homeland Security to support law enforcement efforts to combat issues such as human trafficking, drug smuggling, and threats to critical infrastructure. This is not a contract supporting ICE activities, nor related to ‘surveillance’ as claimed in this inaccurate report. The program compensates AT&T for the cost of analyzing data that falls within the scope of a valid compulsory legal demand and providing the required information to law enforcement pursuant to a court order, search warrant, or subpoena. Like all carriers, AT&T is required by law to respond to valid legal demands, such as subpoenas and court orders. We ensure that these requests are valid, and that our responses comply with the law.”
ICE did not respond to multiple requests for comment, but previously told the Financial Times, “Nothing new here. For years law enforcement across the nation has leveraged technological innovation to fight crime. ICE is no different.”
The precursor to Data Analytical Services was a program called Hemisphere. The New York Times first revealed Hemisphere in 2013, in which AT&T employees sat alongside Drug Enforcement Administration agents and supplied them with phone data going as far back as 1987. Authorities said they stopped federal funding for Hemisphere in September 2024 and shut the program down. But Data Analytical Services is essentially a continuation of that program. The document Senator Wyden’s office previously obtained says that Data Analytical Services was previously called Hemisphere.
“Hemisphere is a surveillance program that refuses to die and keeps coming back with different names and different forms,” Soghoian added. “It is now clear that the Biden White House misled Congress when it said that Hemisphere had been shut down. The White House drug office funded program used by state and local law enforcement may be gone, but federal agencies are continuing to pay AT&T for the same services.”
Update: this piece has been updated to include another statement from AT&T.

UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:21:03 UTC
01:21:03 KST

UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency.
There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all.
That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice.
This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat.
I covered the background to this extensively in my piece, Two-Tier Encryption in the UK. The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging not just to users in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law.
Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information.[1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services. They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so.
The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice, but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice, this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026.
The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs.
At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute”.
The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument.
As Reuters reports, the Tribunal concluded:
“The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.”
The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret.
In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government.
Alice had enabled Advanced Data Protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users, Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection.
Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature.
Our iCloud accounts contain a lot of private information — photos, documents, backups, other material that most of us reasonably expect to remain fully private. Encryption exists so that the service provider shouldn't have the ability to access that information. If a government can compel a technology company to undermine its own protections, the consequences deserve considerably more scrutiny than secret exchanges between officials and lawyers. Today's ruling makes scrutiny more possible.
The Investigatory Powers Act doesn't only exist to regulate Apple's relationship with the UK government. Its provisions establish powers that can potentially be applied to other communications and technology providers. What happens when these powers are used against another company? What happens when the next notice concerns a different service or a different encryption system, or a different category of personal information? How would customers even know about it anyway? That's one of the most troubling aspects of the TCN regime - the secrecy. Companies receiving TCNs can be legally prohibited from disclosing that they have received them.
The UK government’s position, of course, is that these powers are necessary to support lawful investigations and protect public safety. Liberty and Privacy International have thankfully been challenging the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of this regime. They argue it lacks adequate safeguards and threatens fundamental rights. Apple is pursuing its own legal challenge. These cases are now proceeding alongside one another with a substantive hearing expected sometime in 2027. Today's decision doesn't resolve the wider questions, but it does remove one obstacle to examining the dispute in public.
Apple has consistently argued that it will not build ‘backdoors’ into its products. The UK government, meanwhile, has relied on powers that allow it to issue orders to technology companies in secret. For now, the legal process has at least established that the government issued this particular order, but my guess is that we're still some distance from fully understanding what it actually wants Apple to do, and whether it has the legal authority to demand it.
I will continue to follow this one very closely indeed.
- Advanced Data Protection is not synonymous with all iCloud data encryption. Apple already encrypts various categories of iCloud information without ADP, but some of those categories remain accessible to Apple and can potentially be provided in response to valid legal demands. ADP changes that arrangement by extending end-to-end encryption to additional categories of data. ↩︎

UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:21:03 UTC
01:21:03 KST

UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency.
There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all.
That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice.
This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat.
I covered the background to this extensively in my piece, Two-Tier Encryption in the UK. The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging not just to users in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law.
Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information.[1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services. They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so.
The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice, but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice, this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026.
The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs.
At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute”.
The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument.
As Reuters reports, the Tribunal concluded:
“The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.”
The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret.
In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government.
Alice had enabled Advanced Data Protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users, Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection.
Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature.
Our iCloud accounts contain a lot of private information — photos, documents, backups, other material that most of us reasonably expect to remain fully private. Encryption exists so that the service provider shouldn't have the ability to access that information. If a government can compel a technology company to undermine its own protections, the consequences deserve considerably more scrutiny than secret exchanges between officials and lawyers. Today's ruling makes scrutiny more possible.
The Investigatory Powers Act doesn't only exist to regulate Apple's relationship with the UK government. Its provisions establish powers that can potentially be applied to other communications and technology providers. What happens when these powers are used against another company? What happens when the next notice concerns a different service or a different encryption system, or a different category of personal information? How would customers even know about it anyway? That's one of the most troubling aspects of the TCN regime - the secrecy. Companies receiving TCNs can be legally prohibited from disclosing that they have received them.
The UK government’s position, of course, is that these powers are necessary to support lawful investigations and protect public safety. Liberty and Privacy International have thankfully been challenging the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of this regime. They argue it lacks adequate safeguards and threatens fundamental rights. Apple is pursuing its own legal challenge. These cases are now proceeding alongside one another with a substantive hearing expected sometime in 2027. Today's decision doesn't resolve the wider questions, but it does remove one obstacle to examining the dispute in public.

For now, the legal process has at least established that the government issued this particular order, but my guess is that we're still some distance from fully understanding what it actually wants Apple to do, and whether it has the legal authority to demand it.
I will continue to follow this one very closely indeed.

ADP changes that arrangement by extending end-to-end encryption to additional categories of data. ↩︎

Google Chrome dev team declares bug report bankruptcy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:20:12 UTC
01:20:12 KST

Wed, 18 Nov 2026
Google Chrome dev team declares bug report bankruptcy
[ I wrote this in August 2012 and then forgot about it. ]
About 18 months ago I filed a report for a bug in Google Chrome. It wasn't a very important bug. I reported that when Chrome was asked to inline an image, and the image turned out to be in the obscure and seldom-used X-bitmap format, it came up as a "broken image" icon (which isn't a bug) and failed to display the alt text from the img tag (which is).
I then forgot about it until this week, when I got a notice that the report was being closed because it was "obsolete". I was invited to resubmit the bug report if I considered it valid.
My first draft of this article continued politely "The Chrome dev team botched this in a number of ways." That draft came out boring, weak, and vague, so I'm going to try continuing a different way.
That was a really jerky thing to do. I put in my time and trouble to construct a clear bug report with an easy test case; the bug report contained a link to a page that demonstrated the problem. To see if the problem is still present, all you have to do is click the link in the bug report.
But after I spent my time and effort to submit this bug report, Chrome dev decided to ignore it. After they had ignored it for a year and a half, they decided to pitch it in the trash. But if I want, I can submit it again. Now why on earth would I want to do that? Does Chrome think I enjoy assembling bug reports? Maybe I do it for fun? No. The bug report has no value to me. It was an expense. It was a donation to someone I thought would appreciate it. Suppose my neighbor has a boat. Sometimes he lets me use the boat, but it leaks. One day he asks if I will help me fix the boat. I spend the day in his garage painting and sealing some new boards to put into the bottom of the boat. Some time later, I see he has put the new boards into the trash. "What did you do that for?" I ask. He shrugs. "I don't really care if the boat leaks," he says. "But if you want to come over and paint and seal some more boards, how about next week?" Sorry, what am I supposed to get out of this transaction? Chrome dev says they have 40,000 bug reports, too many to deal with. So what? Autoclosing them isn't dealing with them either; it's throwing them in the trash. If having you don't want to get bug reports, yo udon't have to solicit them. They say that a lot of the reports are useless. I'm sure that's true. Most people don't file very good bug reports. A few people do. Who gets pissed off when you throw all the reports into the trash? The people who put in the most effort, that's who. So if you're trying to adopt a strategy that will ensure that your next 40,000 reports are even worse, this is the strategy to adopt. What should Chrome have done here? There is an easy thing and a hard thing.
The easy thing not to say "We threw away your report, but if you think it was a good one, please start over and resubmit it," which is likely to piss off anyone with any sense. Instead, you stick a button on the web site and say "We threw away your report, but if you think it was a good one, please click the button." I would not object to checking if the report was still valid, and clicking a button to reactivate it. The harder thing that they should have done was to not close the reports at all. Managing bug reports is hard. Perl was years behind on bug reports for many years. Many of those reports were indeed obsolete. But there is no cost to keeping them around.
Addenda
- A Mastodon colleague was complaining today about a similar practice, and I wanted to refer him to this article, but couldn't because I had completely forgotten to publish it.
- JWZ complained about something similar in 2003.

At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:19:41 UTC
01:19:41 KST

As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressure and would “remain under human control.”
Reading the speech from a printout, the CEO began by talking about Anthropic’s origins as a way to build powerful technology to help humanity — something that he said was inspired by the loss of his father to a disease that became curable just a few years later.
He acknowledged that while human intelligence had made diseases like the plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world, there were still too few scientists with too little time to make progress in other areas of disease. AI, he said, could help with this by working in concert with humans to further medical progress.
It’s telling that Amodei began with a story highlighting AI’s potentially lifesaving applications, since he’s warned repeatedly about the risks of advancing the technology too quickly. In September, Amodei drew headlines when he outlined a plan to pace AI development, which included things like coordinating with other leading companies on safety standards and embedding evaluators from third-party organizations to verify that companies were following their safety commitments.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, and xAI owner Elon Musk said they agreed with Amodei’s position, although few concrete commitments have been made.
In this morning’s speech, Amodei again stressed the need to progress AI technology and the safety required in doing so. He referred to the “very real risks” of AI in the hands of bad actors, whether those were individuals or nation-states, and the potential for things like “economic disruption” and “losing control of AI systems.”
Anthropic believes these risks are avoidable, he noted, as long as there are safeguards in place. Amodei said the company would continue to be invested in the work of AI alignment and testing, and developing new ways to understand AI behavior so it could remain under human control.
“There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us,” he said. “The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double and triple checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.”
“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei concluded.
His sister, Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, noting that while the risks were real, the promise of AI was also “incredible.”
“We were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks, and I think we have to date done an incredible job doing that. We obviously have more work ahead of us, but we are deeply committed to safety,” she added. 
The full text of Dario Amodei’s opening speech is below:
Thank you, Daniela. My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind. Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that just a few years later became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments. So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket — tools for gene editing, tools for gene synthesis, tools for controlling brain cells with light — started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking, from intelligence.
Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades. It took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR. Nature is full of these patterns, but we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them. Too few scientists with too [little] time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.
I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time, and although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by a few years. Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many other applications of Claude. Our customers, the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth, lift people out of poverty, protect democracy and free societies, even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them, and I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.
At the same time, we’ve always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or by nation-states to economic disruption to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable and we are building anyway, but because we think they are avoidable and we can avoid them. Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic’s DNA from the start, from safeguards against biological and cyber risks to alignment training and testing to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI and keeping it under human control. There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us, the incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.
And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control, we will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing. If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.
When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models. Everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so. But the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better. Thank you.

JPMorgan Chase says its third-party vendors suffered a cyberattack, exposing marketing data like customer names and email addresses. The confirmation follows a report from Cybernews, which says a ransomware group leaked email addresses belonging to around 16,000 JPMorgan Chase customers.
JPMorgan Chase reveals data breach, but says it’s unrelated to this week’s banking outage
Visa and Mastercard were also impacted by a data breach.
In a post about the attack, JPMorgan Chase says “there is no connection” to the outage that occurred earlier this week, which the company attributed to a “software bug:”
We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack. Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.
There is no disruption to our services. Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week.
As reported by Cybernews, the leaked dataset appears to include information linked to JPMorgan Chase’s invitation-only Reserve program.
The hacking group claiming responsibility for the breach says it targeted Visa and Mastercard as well, both of which confirmed attacks on a third-party vendor, Cybernews reports. “There is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected,” Visa says in a statement to Cybernews. Meanwhile, Mastercard spokesperson Seth Eisen tells The Verge that the breach exposed “a limited amount of email addresses” belonging to a “small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program.”
Cybernews says it uncovered datasets connected to 6,000 premium Visa customers, as well as around 2,000 Mastercard customers, if authentic.

Microsoft Testing Remote Lock For Lost Or Stolen Windows Devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Microsoft Testing Remote Lock For Lost Or Stolen Windows Devices (bleepingcomputer.com) 44
			
		 	
				joshuark quotes a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels.
Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked.  "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."

Why AI Wants to Be Local – With Pete Warden (Creator of Moonshine Voice)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
15:38:12 UTC
00:38:12 KST

Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware.
Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube •  AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon •  RSS.
Pete Warden, co-creator of Moonshine Voice and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on Generative AI in the Real World, a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.]
Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:
Related content:
- A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel.
- Hacker News thread for this episode
- The local AI question I had backwards
- I changed my mind about world models
- Previewing the Debate Over Frontier AI Regulation
- Your Model Is Not Your Moat
- Richard Ho → Inside OpenAI’s First Chip
- Joel Hron → Why Build Your Own AI Model When Frontier Models Already Exist?
- Pete Warden → TinyML, Sensor-Driven AI, and Advances in Large Language Models
