Cooling buildings is overtaking heating them as an energy need, IEA says
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
15:57:14 CET
23:57:14 KST

The energy needed to cool the world’s buildings is overtaking the energy needed to heat them for the first time in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on November 19, 2026. The IEA, an intergovernmental agency that advises governments on energy, made the finding in the World Energy Outlook 2026, its main annual report. “Already today, for the first time in energy history, demand for cooling in buildings is overtaking that for heating,” the report’s executive summary says.
Two forces drive the change: rising incomes and rising temperatures. In emerging and developing economies outside China, 85% of households are exposed to high temperatures for at least part of the year. Fewer than one in five households there own an air conditioner.
In the IEA’s main scenario, a projection built on the policies governments have announced, the electricity used for cooling worldwide grows by 1,700 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2035. A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours; the kilowatt-hour is the unit on a household power bill. That increase is roughly India’s total electricity demand today.
A first in energy history
The IEA’s press release calls the shift “a striking milestone”: “energy needs to keep buildings cool are now overtaking energy needs for heating them for the first time in history.”
Most of this year’s report deals with the oil and gas shock caused by disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The cooling finding comes from another part of the report, on what people use energy for: getting around, heating, cooling and computing. The IEA calls these uses energy services.
Of these services, cooling adds the most new demand. Cooling demand in buildings has risen 55% since 2015, the IEA says in its full report. In every scenario the agency models, cooling accounts for more than 40% of the growth in energy services worldwide through 2035.
That growth comes mostly from hot countries that are getting richer. It also comes from places where cooling used to be a minor need. The report names Europe, where heat waves and warmer summers are turning cooling into a new source of demand. It cites record heat waves there and strong air conditioner sales in European countries that historically needed little cooling.
The IEA notes that August 2026 was the hottest month on record worldwide. Since mid-June, the sea surface has also set a heat record for the date every day.
Who has air conditioning, and who doesn’t
Air conditioner ownership varies widely. In Australia, Japan and the United States, around 90% of households own at least one unit, according to the report. In India and Indonesia, fewer than one in five do, despite high cooling needs. Worldwide, around 80% of the population lives in places that need cooling for at least part of the year, and around 40% of households own an air conditioner.
In emerging and developing economies outside China, the IEA projects that ownership will rise from under 20% of households today to 32% by 2035 and 45% by 2050. The projection is the same in all its scenarios. The IEA also models a current policies scenario, which counts only the policies already in place. In that scenario, more than 85% of the growth in the world’s stock of home air conditioners over the next decade happens in emerging and developing economies, China included.
By the middle of the century, the IEA projects, the world’s buildings will have more cooled floor space than heated floor space.
More electricity for cooling, and a heat-wave what-if
In the main scenario, which the IEA calls the Stated Policies Scenario, the electricity used to cool buildings rises by 1,700 TWh by 2035. It goes from about 3,000 TWh a year today to 4,700 TWh a year.
The report also models a “heatwave case,” a what-if kept apart from the main scenario. In it, heat waves become stronger, more frequent and longer, so more households buy air conditioners and use them more. In that case, cooling demand grows by 700 TWh more than in the main scenario by 2035. That is 40% more growth.
Cooling also weighs more on power grids than its share of total use suggests. Air conditioners run hardest at the same time, on the hottest days. That drives up peak demand, the highest demand a grid must meet during the year. In the main scenario, cooling makes up only 12% of the world’s electricity demand in 2035, but 30% of peak demand.
Peak demand is measured in gigawatts (GW), which count power at a single moment, while terawatt-hours count energy used over a period. Added up across the world’s power systems, it is 4,700 GW today. It grows by about 40% by 2035, in both the main scenario and the current policies scenario. Under current policies, the cooling part of the peak alone grows by 720 GW, more than India’s entire power generating capacity today.
In the main scenario, cooling and appliances together add 2,900 TWh of electricity demand by 2035. That is more electricity than the whole European Union uses today. Almost 90% of that growth happens in emerging and developing economies.
Heating still consumes more energy
Measured by the fuel and electricity consumed, heating is still well ahead. “Globally, there is less cooling than heating demand, but more electric cooling than electric heating demand,” the report says in its section on buildings. Space heating, which keeps rooms warm, uses about a third of all the energy consumed in buildings, more than any other use.
The milestone uses a different yardstick. In the report’s framing, the comparison is about energy services, meaning the comfort delivered. The sentence about cooling overtaking heating sits in the report’s section on demand for energy services. The IEA measures those services as “useful energy”: the energy that does the job people want, such as “the heat produced by a heater.”
By our reading, the two findings fit together because of how the equipment works. A boiler burns fuel and loses part of its energy in the process. An air conditioner, like a heat pump, moves heat from one place to another, so it delivers more cooling than the electricity it consumes.
The report counts air conditioners and heat pumps as devices whose output exceeds the energy they take in. That, by our reading, is why cooling can overtake heating in the service delivered while heating still consumes more energy.
The executive summary puts no number on the crossing itself. It is a result of the IEA’s modeling, and the agency describes the crossing as under way (“is overtaking”). None of the report’s scenarios is a forecast, as the IEA’s executive director, Fatih Birol, said in the press release.
In advanced economies, heating remains the largest energy service. It declines only slowly, as better insulation and warmer average temperatures offset the effect of rising incomes.
What it means
Air conditioners are spreading in the countries where most of the world’s people live. In the IEA’s projections, the share of households that own one in emerging and developing economies outside China more than doubles by 2050. Those households gain comfort, and power grids must carry a bigger load in the hottest hours of the year. Electric trucks, cars and heat pumps add to the load on those grids as well.
Electricity already supplied 23% of the energy consumed worldwide in 2025, and the IEA sees that share closing in on 30% by 2035. The agency says at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines are needed over the next ten years. On the supply side, solar covered more of the growth in world energy demand in 2025 than any other source, a first for a renewable source, according to the IEA. In the European Union, solar became the biggest source of electricity over the summer.
Efficiency rules also shape demand. Minimum efficiency standards are the legal floor on how efficient an appliance must be to go on sale. For household appliances such as refrigerators, washing machines, lighting and televisions, the IEA calculates that bringing every country up to the strictest standards in force today would save 800 TWh of electricity by 2035, almost half of it from refrigerators alone. For cooling, the current policies scenario keeps those standards at today’s levels, and cooling demand reaches 4,900 TWh by 2035, compared with 4,700 TWh in the main scenario.
Sources
- As an unprecedented shock reshapes the energy world, its duration will determine the scale of the change, International Energy Agency (press release), November 19, 2026
- World Energy Outlook 2026: Executive summary, International Energy Agency, November 19, 2026
- World Energy Outlook 2026 (full report, PDF), International Energy Agency, November 19, 2026

Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
14:54:39 UTC
23:54:39 KST

Arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the company and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.
Amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes valued around a combined $307.9 billion at the company’s updated IPO price of $83 per share. Amazon, which invested $18 billion into the AI startup, would see its 14.7% stake hit upwards of $159 billion, while Google’s 13.7% stake is valued at nearly $149 billion, according to share ownership figures disclosed in Anthropic’s IPO prospectus.
A handful of other AI infrastructure providers are also positioned to benefit. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC have joined Google in committing $26 billion to Anthropic at its IPO price in a private placement.
In total, Google has invested $12.3 billion into Anthropic since 2023, with another promised $30 billion dependent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. And with the exception of TSMC, Anthropic has announced multibillion-dollar strategic partnerships with its other infrastructure supplier investors — including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Microsoft, and Micron — that would see Anthropic purchasing their products.
This is the circular financing that has made some observers so skeptical of the AI boom. These companies are not just investors; they’re also Anthropic’s biggest suppliers. It might look like Amazon and Google are putting billions into Anthropic, but they get that money right back when Anthropic needs to train a model or serve Claude to users. From afar, it looks like unprecedented revenue growth for cloud companies and unprecedented fundraising from Anthropic — but it’s just the same money passing from one pocket to another.
Today’s IPO marks a critical change in that financing system, the moment it might just become self-sustaining. Those investments appear to have paid off, and are now liquid. Anthropic is still operating at a net loss of tens of billions of dollars each quarter — but it will no longer be suppliers and private investors footing the bill. Now, capital will come from a mix of public-market investors and corporate bonds, neither of which have the conflicts-of-interest that caused concerns before.
And critically, the company’s new bottom line looks pretty good.
Once it debuts, Anthropic is expected to have about $220 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, including proceeds from its IPO and the $26 billion private placement. Anthropic also has the ability to pay for future commitments in stock.
Joey Brookhart, who leads the Tokenomics team at SemiAnalysis, estimates that Anthropic needs roughly $280 billion in cumulative revenue over the next four years to pay for its compute bill, which Brookhart said is “achievable given where they will be next year from a revenue perspective.”
“The ownership stake is very worthwhile, and those companies no longer need any more support from [suppliers],” Brookhart told TechCrunch. “Amazon doesn’t need to prop them up anymore. The revenue is all coming from other customers.”
That doesn’t mean the server bills are going down, though. Anthropic has already committed to spend $900 billion, primarily for compute and infrastructure, according to a regulatory filing. Certain agreements have termination provisions, but Brookhart thinks the company is in a strong position to pay up.
On the other side, Anthropic generated $17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, putting the company on pace for a $68 billion annualized rate for the year. If Anthropic continues to grow at its current trajectory, Brookhart believes it could easily cover the gap needed to fund its compute.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, agreed.
“By the time the IPO is done, Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had,” Luria told TechCrunch, noting that the firm raised around $141 billion in capital and will take home around $91.7 billion in net proceeds at $83 per share. “And they’re not burning cash. They’re just going to have a war chest.”
A public listing will make Anthropic a more credible borrower, making it easier to raise money outside of public markets, says Brookhart. That’s despite recent reports that creditors might not see Anthropic as “investment-grade” material.
Luria distinguished between Anthropic’s supplier investments and neoclouds like CoreWeave, which he sees as more purely supported by circular financing. “CoreWeave wouldn’t exist if Nvidia didn’t prop them up, and it probably won’t exist if Nvidia doesn’t bail them out,” Luria said.
Brookhart also pushed back on describing Anthropic’s financing as purely circular, saying it was still “additive to the ecosystem.”
For both analysts, the biggest risk to Anthropic is simply that it will lose the AI race. Right now, the company’s growth is fueled by its status at the frontier of generative AI — but if it’s overtaken by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or even cheap open-weight models, that could change fast. As Luria put it: “If we’re all using other people’s models, then Anthropic’s not worth a trillion and a half dollars. It’s worth nothing.”
But regardless of who wins the frontier, compute suppliers will likely be just fine. Neither Brookhart nor Luria believe Anthropic’s growth is at risk, despite some arguments that cheaper tokens and more competition will directly affect the AI company’s bottom line.
“For Amazon and Google, the risk isn’t actually that high because in that scenario, we’re using other models,” Luria said. “I’m arguing we’re going to use a lot more AI. I don’t know if it’s all Anthropic’s AI…. That’s still going to come from a data center managed by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.”

Germany and Austria Call for European Control of TikTok
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
14:44:50 UTC
23:44:50 KST

Germany and Austria are calling for a strategic shift in the ownership of TikTok’s European arm, proposing that it be brought under European management.
In a joint statement, representatives of both countries expressed their desire to introduce a corporate structure that guarantees regional oversight of the platform’s algorithms and user data, separating it from its current parent company, Beijing-based ByteDance.
The proposal, described by Germany’s Minister for Culture and Media, Wolfram Weimer, and Austria’s State Secretary for Digital Affairs, Alexander Pröll, as an attempt to ‘Europeanise’ the service, is seeking support from other EU member states.
The move follows a similar precedent set in January, when the United States reached an agreement with ByteDance to establish a joint venture in which American interests hold a majority stake in the app’s domestic operations.
The concept was first introduced by Minister Weimer, who suggested that a consortium of European media companies could take over the platform’s regional operations.
The main motivations behind the move are to safeguard personal data and limit external influence on public debate.
Both officials pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the Chinese government’s potential access to European user data, given ByteDance’s origins.
They also stressed that, since recommendation systems largely determine the visibility and distribution of content, bringing the platform under European ownership would provide essential control over both its technological framework and users’ privacy.

Germany and Austria are calling for a strategic shift in the ownership of TikTok’s European arm, proposing that it be brought under European management.
In a joint statement, representatives of both countries expressed their desire to introduce a corporate structure that guarantees regional oversight of the platform’s algorithms and user data, separating it from its current parent company, Beijing-based ByteDance.
The proposal, described by Germany’s Minister for Culture and Media, Wolfram Weimer, and Austria’s State Secretary for Digital Affairs, Alexander Pröll, as an attempt to ‘Europeanise’ the service, is seeking support from other EU member states.
The move follows a similar precedent set in January, when the United States reached an agreement with ByteDance to establish a joint venture in which American interests hold a majority stake in the app’s domestic operations.
The concept was first introduced by Minister Weimer, who suggested that a consortium of European media companies could take over the platform’s regional operations.
The main motivations behind the move are to safeguard personal data and limit external influence on public debate.
Both officials pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the Chinese government’s potential access to European user data, given ByteDance’s origins.
They also stressed that, since recommendation systems largely determine the visibility and distribution of content, bringing the platform under European ownership would provide essential control over both its technological framework and users’ privacy.

With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
14:26:20 UTC
23:26:20 KST

Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.
With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
Anthropic’s unusual power structure gives it free rein to shape AI’s future.
With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
Anthropic’s unusual power structure gives it free rein to shape AI’s future.
Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.
One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.
Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.”
The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi.
Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog.
Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.”
Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?”
Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement.
But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed necessary, and even after its restructuring, they retained that ability for safety and security matters, such as delaying or stopping a model release. Anthropic’s Form S-1 suggests that the LTBT, with its main duty being appointing (and potentially removing) certain board members, does not have either of those levels of authority.
Instead, Anthropic’s structure looks more like the kind of founder-centric setup that Silicon Valley favors — like Mark Zuckerberg with Meta, and Elon Musk with SpaceX.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
“Neither the Trust or the trustees have any decisionmaking authority … over day to day decisions,” said Hamza Chaudhry, who leads AI and national security at the Future of Life Institute. “So I do not have strong hopes for the LTBT being a key mechanism for governance after they go public.”
The former Anthropic employee said that Anthropic’s founders are essentially the only ones with any real decisionmaking power: “I would be surprised if you could find anyone who knows the founders, knows the Long-Term Benefit Trust, understands how decisions get made, and thinks the Long-Term Benefit Trust has any meaningful power,” he said. The employee added that the trustees were both “poorly equipped to provide meaningful oversight” to the founders and also selected on purpose to not rock the boat.
Anthropic as a public company will face more pressure than ever before to secure capital, whether via driving more revenue or fundraising. That means that, as has been a trend in the industry for years, it will likely be more difficult to justify expensive AI safety initiatives, and there will inevitably be more pressure to speed up product releases and commercialization. “This trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power,” Lipton said. “So you either trust that they are going to balance the interests of society appropriately, or you don’t. Either way, the real constraint on whatever societal impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money.”
Anthropic has been open about the fact that it’s in extreme need of cold, hard cash, particularly to buy more compute and speed up its AI advancement. “Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces,” Amodei said last Friday in a livestreamed conversation with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. “If you buy too much, of course you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers, and even more importantly … you can’t do the R&D.”
Anthropic’s website summarizes the company’s raison d’être as one thing: “AI research and products that put safety at the frontier.” But it’s also been clear that for that safety pledge to matter, Anthropic needs vast resources to remain a viable business. Like other labs, it’s been pursuing recursive self-improvement, a controversial and potentially dangerous industry milestone denoting AI systems that can autonomously improve and create advanced versions of themselves. “You can’t do safety from second place,” said Anthropic policy chief Sarah Heck in September.
This explanation hasn’t satisfied everyone, including some Anthropic employees. Anthropic’s head of safeguards research departed in February alleging that “the world is in peril”; one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, made headlines in September for claiming that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”; and that same month, an Anthropic safety researcher departed for a job at nonprofit third-party AI auditor METR, writing that “AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society” and that “while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the HuggingFace attack [by OpenAI agents], I think that’s partly a matter of luck.”
Are you a current or former Anthropic employee? Contact me via Signal at haydenfield.11 on a non-work device with tips.
On Wednesday, a new statement from the Center for AI Safety, with prominent industry signatories from Hugging Face, Harvard University, and more, alleged that Anthropic is “not a safe AI company” and that it attempts to “amass power in the name of the greater good.” It stated, “Anthropic warns that recursively self-improving AI could concentrate power and escape human control, yet races to build it first. The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public—even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation.”
The former Anthropic employee said he felt he had initially “drunk the Kool-Aid” about Anthropic needing to come in first place in the AI race for a safe outcome but then grew disillusioned, realizing that the race to the top did not “warrant the cost imposed” — namely, that one company should not be able to “unilaterally” decide to pursue RSI. (Amodei has stated publicly that “left unchecked, [RSI] could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”)
“It’s pretty ridiculous that private companies are building a new form of intelligence on track to be more powerful and influential on the planet than humans and are doing that with less oversight, in many ways, than taco trucks currently have,” the former employee said.
Anthropic’s website states that “at the end of the day, the mission is what we’re all here for. It gives us a shared purpose and allows us to act swiftly together, rather than being pulled in multiple directions by competing goals. It engenders trust and collaboration, and is the final arbiter in our decisions.” The question is whether, and how, the interpretation of Anthropic’s mission may shift — once it’s facing more pressure than ever before to justify a fully diluted market cap of about $1.5 trillion.

OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
14:20:08 UTC
23:20:08 KST

October 27, 2026 · kixelated
OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
On a previous episode, I flamed OpenAI for using WebRTC and it went viral on Hacker News.
thx
A huge shoutout to Sean DuBois and Justin Uberti (WebRTC experts at OpenAI) for reaching out after my unhinged rant.
You could have just said @kixelated ur dumb but you didn’t.
Alas, my divinely anointed crusade against WebRTC is not over. deus vult
Hot Take Alert
Let’s say you’re a vibe coder at a frontier lab working on a voice AI product.
Let’s say you’re making (and burning) an obscene amount of cash.
Let’s say one of your users vocalizes: what is le capital of France?
If your AI ever replies with:
I’m sorry, you broke up, can you repeat that?
You fucked up. You picked WebRTC for voice AI.
The Danger that Lurks Beneath
You boot up your favorite application: ChatGPT™. You click on the microphone and grunt:
What is le capital of France?
OH NO, hypothetical sudden packet loss. A kraken nibbles on some underwater cable. All too common I’m afraid.
WebRTC is designed for conference calls, aka real humans and real voices. It is hyper aggressive and will drop any late audio packets to keep latency real-time. Just like Leonardo DiCaprio, anything above 30ms is too old.
This kind of sucks for a voice AI product. You walk out of wifi range, hit a cellular dead zone, or starlink terminal switches satellites. Oops, your tokens are wasted, or worse, AI tries to guess what you said.
WebRTC can usually detect packet loss and retransmit. But retransmissions are disabled by default for audio. And even when enabled, the audio jitter buffer won’t wait for them.
But why not? Isn’t this networking 101? Just send that shit again?
It’s because of us.
The Speed of You
We flesh bags consume/produce audio in “real-time”, aka a human clock rate. Our neurons can only fire so fast.
For a real-time conferencing product like Google Meet, latency needs to be near zero. Any delay is super fucking annoying, which is why WebRTC does everything in its power to minimize it.
Blocking on retransmissions will cause delays. It’s the fatal flaw with TCP and why WebRTC is UDP based in the first place. And worse yet, retransmissions will cause a rapid burst of audio on recovery.
This is a bad user experience. Humans do not want to wait, then process a burst of audio at 10x speed. WebRTC instead primarily* relies on human retransmissions.
You: What is le … France?
Me:
You: I said, what is le capital of France?
* Before a WebRTC warrior flames me on LinkedIn, read the fix it fix it fix it section.
Are we doomed to mediocrity?
Clock That Solder Boy
Of course not. Wake up old man, it’s not 2020 any longer. The internet is no longer for our flabby lips.
Our robot overlords produce/consume audio based on a silicon clock rate. We shoved electricity into a rock and now it can read a library in minutes. What a time to be alive.
Voice agents can hear and speak audio faster than real-time.
Listening at 20x the speed? No problem.
Speaking at 20x the speed? No problem.
Humans stuck at real-time.
We speak too slowly, so speech-to-text has to wait for us.
We hear too slowly, so text-to-speech has to wait for us.
WebRTC is designed for humans, not voice AI agents. These poor robots are being held back by our mediocrity.
I Require Context
When it comes to LLMs, latency budgets get weird.
Normally you would think of latency as the amount of time it takes for a grunt to traverse a tin can. However, LLMs are blocked on context.
Here’s a dumb example of context growing over time:
- 1s: What
- 2s: What is
- 3s: What is le
- 4s: What is le capital
- 5s: What is le capital of
- 6s: What is le capital of France?
If an LLM tries to answer my prompt before getting the full context, shit will suck. France is le gatekeeper, and everything before it is effectively a prerequisite. In this example, what matters is the latency of the last packet.
Those poor packets that were attacken by the kraken? WebRTC actually had seconds to retransmit with no latency penalty. The AI agent can process faster than real-time to catch up without the end user (aka YOU) noticing a thing.
So that’s what Mr. MoQ does. No packet left behind: we keep retransmitting until the AI actually needs the audio.
It’s not expensive either: audio is tiny. 1s of Opus @ 64Kbps is 8KB, originally sent as 50 tiny packets, but it can be retransmitted as ~6 QUIC packets. We have literal seconds to retransmit 6 packets to avoid any user impact.
And if we manage to accomplish this herculean task: all the context arrives in time!
The model no longer has to guess. It no longer has to be trained on silence or distortion either. This is a pure user experience win.
Not Just Mics
Guess what? WebRTC doesn’t just suck for STT, it also sucks for TTS.
Fun Fact: WebRTC renders audio (and video) based on when it arrives, not when it is supposed to be rendered. Every other protocol uses timestamps, but Mr. WebRTC barely looks at them, because accuracy is a non-goal. Sure, it’ll nudge audio and video into sync by a few milliseconds, but good luck sending the video 500ms after the audio.
This is a huge problem for voice AI. TTS is generated faster than real-time, stamping each packet with a future timestamp. But in order to play back audio at the correct time with WebRTC… the agent needs to sleep before transmitting each packet.
And if there’s any packet loss, our TTS is lost, will never be retransmitted, tokens burned, yada yada.
If only there was some way to signal when to render each audio packet. A stamp of sorts.
Random Access Memory
Welcome back to the future Marty. We faster than real-time now.
RAM has this amazing property of being stupidly expensive. And being able to store stuff locally. You know, like audio that needs to be played over the speakers.
We put a timestamp on each audio frame and use that to determine when to play it out of RAM. Absurd, I know.
It’s how the Youtubes keeps playing back video even when you lose network connectivity. MoQ does the same thing but for voice AI. Your sick baking recipe won’t be subject to surprise congestion.
And don’t you fret, 2 minutes of audio is only 1MB. You’re not going to have to take out a loan to buy another RAM stick.
Disclaimer: this behavior is not IETF standardized. It’s something only my moq.dev clients (and thus Pipecat) support. Be my guest if you want to argue with Cisco and get it into the official standards.
Enter the Antagonist
Then why is OpenAI using WebRTC?
WebRTC is the state of the art for real-time, conversational audio.
It’s available in every browser via libwebrtc, a C++ monolith maintained by Google.
It’s so complicated and sophisticated that Safari and Firefox use libwebrtc too, rather than vibe code their own like everything else.
The problem is that WebRTC is the Google Meet client. It is designed specifically for Google’s conferencing product, not their voice AI product (they use WebSocket), and certainly not your product.
quite the anti-competitive ruse tbh. Google can ship product updates without consulting the other browser vendors. No other conferencing app can do this on the web.
Fun Fact: This is why every other conferencing app recommends a native client. Otherwise, they can only reach parity with Google Meet at best. Native apps can do whatever they want over UDP instead.
Fix It Fix It Fix It
So that’s why your hyper deluxe ChatGPT™ voice AI model, after billions invested, has the audacity to ask: can you repeat that?
I could dump on WebRTC for days, but I want to be positive for a change. Here’s how to fix it.
First off, I need to acknowledge what WebRTC does have:
- NetEQ is amazing. It changes audio playback speed based on jitter. But not packet loss.
- Audio retransmissions can now be enabled via SDP munging (disgusting). But the NetEQ jitter buffer won’t wait for them.
- The playout-delay RTP extension is perfect for voice AI. But it’s video only.
To fix WebRTC, we need to petition Google to:
- Implement playout-delay for audio.
- Allow the jitter buffer to grow, both in the past and into the future (for TTS).
- Render audio based on timestamps not vibes.
- IDK some RTP extension to bump the track generation (for interruptions).
And of course, petition the wider WebRTC ecosystem to do the same.
Gatekept
The main problem with WebRTC will remain: Google is the gatekeeper.
Your Claude friend can’t just fork libwebrtc and fix these issues.
Google is required for web support, at least until Theo spends $420k to rewrite Chromium in Rust.
I think it’s amazing that playout-delay was merged 10 years ago and audio still doesn’t have it. Higher latency/quality playback has never been a priority for WebRTC, since Google Meet is the only product that matters.
Fun Fact: This is why I ended up creating MoQ. We tried using WebRTC at Twitch but the real-time-or-else made for a poor user experience. I am but a humble software engineer, and despite trying, we failed to petition Google.
But OpenAI has enough sway to fix WebRTC. One long-deserved improvement is WARP (not that WARP), which was hot on the heels of my last blog post. Keep at it Justin, or join the Dark Side with me.
Enter The Protagonist
In my humble and handsome opinion, it’s time to invest in a better transport. Take a few of the M’s from the B’s and T’s; nobody will notice.
A voice agent should never ask the user to retransmit a prompt.
A voice agent should instead ask the transport to retransmit a prompt.
Spoiler alert: Media over QUIC is that better transport btw.
Pipecat now supports MoQ! A huge thank you to Vanessa and Claude Code for putting in the work and putting up with my constant “improvements”.
Here’s a crude demo with my credit card deets attached. please don’t milk me dry.
Note that I’ve only spent like a day of work prompting on this.
It took me significantly longer to write this damn blog post.
Don’t judge too harshly pls.
And yes, it sometimes says “can you repeat that?” which is hilariously ironic. The first/last hop is MoQ, but I don’t control the rest of the pipeline. If Deepgram, OpenAI, or Cartesia drop ur packets then there’s nothing I can do about it.
Interruptions
We’re not done yet. I wanted to shill the MoQ in the middle of the blog and use the rest…
Sometimes the AI is monologuing and you need to tell it to STFU. It’s pretty easy to do with WebRTC because of the sleep before sending each packet. But with MoQ, we need some signal to tell the player to abandon the playout buffer.
Here’s the naive approach without a signal:
notdo this on my first implementation.
My solution for this is deviously clever. So clever.
For MoQ, we’ve prioritized the ability to add/remove tracks dynamically. Most media protocols have fixed tracks and it’s a pain in the butt: HLS, DASH, RTMP, WebRTC, etc. You can’t add 1080p, or switch codecs, after a broadcast is live.
My super clever idea is to reuse this functionality for interruptions. Just make a new audio track (and remove the old one) as the STFU Signal™.
This works on a generic MoQ player. We automatically switch tracks, using timestamps to keep synchronization.
ez
Butt-to-Butt
Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. You didn’t mention speech-to-speech?
Look, Dunning-Kruger is the only reason the previous blog post exists. I didn’t know speech-to-speech existed until the comment section. What can I say but ur welcome.
DISCLAIMER: I still haven’t done any research on the state of voice AI.
I give you full permission to tweet @kixelated ur stupid.
The idea behind speech-to-speech is to cut out the text middleman. The disjoint STT -> LLM -> TTS pipelines get smashed together, reducing latency while preserving verbal context. OpenAI is the pioneer in this space and they deserve mad props.
So this vindicates WebRTC right? The speech-to-speech latency can be low enough to justify dropping packets?
Not so fast literary strawman. There’s a fundamental trade-off between latency and quality.
Latency Budgets
The more time you have to work on something, the better the result.
Good things take time, like Fable changing a single line in README.md because I’m too poor to pay 3.5x for ultrafast.
Networks are the same. The more time you have to transmit something, the better the quality. It’s why retransmits exist in the first place.
Unless you’re doing broadcast TV, which still uses MPEG-TS and still results in glitchy messes. Seriously wtf guys, TV is no longer over the air, and we don’t need 188 byte packets any longer.
Anyway, the amount of time a user is willing to wait for something is a product decision. Put on your big boye pants, it’s time to be a PM. Do users want something fast and lossy, or slow and reliable?
Why not both?
That’s the idea behind speech-to-speech. Do a low-latency STS pass for easy prompts and to generate filler noise.
Human: What is le capital of France?
ChatGPT: One second, let me look that up.
Boom, even that useless “I’m thinking” response makes the human feel good chemicals. But more importantly for us anti-PMs, it buys us enough time to start a slower pass.
I don’t work at a frontier lab so this is all speculation, but I imagine STT->LLM->TTS is still used for these slower passes. A STS model with Astra/Fable quality is absolutely ideal… but probably not worth the investment.
Either way, doesn’t matter if it’s STS or STT->LLM->TTS. The only thing that matters is the latency budget.
MoQ do Both
One of the core problems we’re trying to fix with MoQ is the whole “one transport per latency” issue in the industry. It’s face-palmingly common to use different protocols based on the latency budget.
For example, an all-hands presentation where the speakers use Zoom, while everybody else watches via HLS and can’t participate.
Fuck that noise, MoQ supports multiple latency targets with a single connection. In the case of voice AI:
- real-time latency for rapid replies (STS).
- loss-less quality for slow replies (STT->LLM->TTS).
How? Every MoQ subscription includes how long the subscriber is willing to wait.
Your real-time model can have a maximum latency of 500ms while your more accurate model might have a maximum latency of 5s. Both get coalesced into a single upstream subscription which can fanout.
And note that this is the maximum latency. The latency is 0 except during terrible network conditions, and eventually we give up. This is the core difference between MoQ and TCP/WebSocket for Voice AI.
Your transport latency should be aligned with your product latency budget.
It’s Simple: Predict the Future
One more strawman to beat into the dirt.
Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. WebRTC doesn’t care about packet loss because it uses FEC.
M8 go read my previous blog posts: never use datagrams and forward error correction. This is like my dumber one hot take.
WebRTC (and Opus) include Forward Error Correction to help mask packet loss. The idea is to stuff a crappier, lower bitrate copy of the previous audio frame into the next packet.
But only a single last packet. It can’t even handle two lost packets in a row, let alone a full network blip.
This is fine for WebRTC because it doesn’t give a shit about audio older than 30ms. But it’s not fine for voice AI or really anything on the internet. Packet loss due to congestion is bursty, not random.
A common “fix” is to spread these copies over time, so you can handle X lost packets in a row. See Opus 1.5. All of this extra data has a real cost, and if you don’t know what you’re doing (and you don’t), then you will aggravate bufferbloat.
In my humble (and attractive) opinion, FEC is best for huge RTTs, like transmitting to le moon.
In <current year>, we instead use CDNs to shrink the lossy first/last mile which makes retransmissions OP.
Why send more bytes spread over 400ms, instead of retransmitting in 40ms?
But if a WebRTC warrior insists, QUIC libraries can retransmit stream data as many times as they want. Basically RED but based on byte offsets, not packets, and fully transparent to the receiver. That’s a free idea btw.
More Free Ideas

Decouple Compute
I know you have obscene amounts of capital, but getting GPUs next to every single user in the world is hard. But getting cheap DELL servers next to every single user in the world is easy.
- Run moq-relay within CDN edges.
- Run models where GPUs are available.
Like I said earlier, this is basically the premise of CDNs. A huge number of edge nodes close to users minimizes the congested first/last mile. Over-provision the backbone so you can get the traffic to the GPUs without congestion.
You can independently scale network and compute.
Which I hope you guys already do, and are big enough to justify a custom Voice AI protocol instead of using a standardized MoQ implementation.
For everybody else, MoQ is generic enough to serve more than just Voice AI. Think of MoQ like a live HTTP. It’s an IETF standard after all, the same body that does that HTTP thing.
In fact, my first big customer is using moq.pro to mass fanout JSON blobs. Literally a generic pub/sub protocol masquerading as an A/V protocol.
Prioritize Context
I’m a transport and ideas guy, not an AI scientist. Don’t flame me if this is obvious and/or impossible.
The core problem with WebRTC+AI is that there’s a disconnect between the model and the transport. This blog focused on aligning latency… but what about aligning context?
After all, not all tokens have the same weight. If we knew the relative importance of each token, we could use that to make informed networking decisions.
high priority: what capital france
low priority: is le
zero priority: <silence>
To implement this via MoQ, you would split the audio track into separate tracks that are encoded independently. The high priority track would get first dibs on available bandwidth, and the subscriber would wait longer for it.
But TBH the hard part is actually giving a shit. Audio bitrates are so low that you rarely get a chance to prioritize anyway, and it’s not worth the hassle of doing a client-side tokenizer. Maybe it could matter for video tho.
Back-fill that Boye
The other problem with dropping audio after 30ms is that it’s a one-way door.
Bold prediction: The next Claudism will be one-way door after it’s been trained on this post.
Once a network transport decides to drop data over the network, it can’t be used for other things. Now, I don’t know if frontier labs store raw audio… but maybe they should.
Eventually the AI model has to stop waiting and guess based on incomplete data. Did it do a good job or bad job? How can we know?
Well… maybe don’t actually drop the audio; keep that shit in RAM.
Audio is tiny after all.
We can set max-latency to 10 minutes and it will be transmitted eventually at the lowest priority.
We backfill that boye only when the network has fully recovered.
Why backfill via MoQ? Why not save it as a file and train on it later?
Vroom vroom, the GPU is warm. Ask the model if it did a good job guessing what the user said X seconds ago while the context is cached. Use it as training data. IDK I’m not a scientist.

OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
14:20:08 UTC
23:20:08 KST

October 27, 2026 · kixelated
OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
On a previous episode, I flamed OpenAI for using WebRTC and it went viral on Hacker News.
thx
A huge shoutout to Sean DuBois and Justin Uberti (WebRTC experts at OpenAI) for reaching out after my unhinged rant.
You could have just said @kixelated ur dumb but you didn’t.
Alas, my divinely anointed crusade against WebRTC is not over. deus vult
Hot Take Alert
Let’s say you’re a vibe coder at a frontier lab working on a voice AI product.
Let’s say you’re making (and burning) an obscene amount of cash.
Let’s say one of your users vocalizes: what is le capital of France?
If your AI ever replies with:
I’m sorry, you broke up, can you repeat that?
You fucked up. You picked WebRTC for voice AI.
The Danger that Lurks Beneath
You boot up your favorite application: ChatGPT™. You click on the microphone and grunt:
What is le capital of France?
OH NO, hypothetical sudden packet loss. A kraken nibbles on some underwater cable. All too common I’m afraid.
WebRTC is designed for conference calls, aka real humans and real voices. It is hyper aggressive and will drop any late audio packets to keep latency real-time. Just like Leonardo DiCaprio, anything above 30ms is too old.
This kind of sucks for a voice AI product. You walk out of wifi range, hit a cellular dead zone, or starlink terminal switches satellites. Oops, your tokens are wasted, or worse, AI tries to guess what you said.
WebRTC can usually detect packet loss and retransmit. But retransmissions are disabled by default for audio. And even when enabled, the audio jitter buffer won’t wait for them.
But why not? Isn’t this networking 101? Just send that shit again?
It’s because of us.
The Speed of You
We flesh bags consume/produce audio in “real-time”, aka a human clock rate. Our neurons can only fire so fast.
For a real-time conferencing product like Google Meet, latency needs to be near zero. Any delay is super fucking annoying, which is why WebRTC does everything in its power to minimize it.
Blocking on retransmissions will cause delays. It’s the fatal flaw with TCP and why WebRTC is UDP based in the first place. And worse yet, retransmissions will cause a rapid burst of audio on recovery.
This is a bad user experience. Humans do not want to wait, then process a burst of audio at 10x speed. WebRTC instead primarily* relies on human retransmissions.
You: What is le … France?
Me:
You: I said, what is le capital of France?
* Before a WebRTC warrior flames me on LinkedIn, read the fix it fix it fix it section.
Are we doomed to mediocrity?
Clock That Solder Boy
Of course not. Wake up old man, it’s not 2020 any longer. The internet is no longer for our flabby lips.
Our robot overlords produce/consume audio based on a silicon clock rate. We shoved electricity into a rock and now it can read a library in minutes. What a time to be alive.
Voice agents can hear and speak audio faster than real-time.
Listening at 20x the speed? No problem.
Speaking at 20x the speed? No problem.
Humans stuck at real-time.
We speak too slowly, so speech-to-text has to wait for us.
We hear too slowly, so text-to-speech has to wait for us.
WebRTC is designed for humans, not voice AI agents. These poor robots are being held back by our mediocrity.
I Require Context
When it comes to LLMs, latency budgets get weird.
Normally you would think of latency as the amount of time it takes for a grunt to traverse a tin can. However, LLMs are blocked on context.
Here’s a dumb example of context growing over time:
- 1s: What
- 2s: What is
- 3s: What is le
- 4s: What is le capital
- 5s: What is le capital of
- 6s: What is le capital of France?
If an LLM tries to answer my prompt before getting the full context, shit will suck. France is le gatekeeper, and everything before it is effectively a prerequisite. In this example, what matters is the latency of the last packet.
Those poor packets that were attacken by the kraken? WebRTC actually had seconds to retransmit with no latency penalty. The AI agent can process faster than real-time to catch up without the end user (aka YOU) noticing a thing.
So that’s what Mr. MoQ does. No packet left behind: we keep retransmitting until the AI actually needs the audio.
It’s not expensive either: audio is tiny. 1s of Opus @ 64Kbps is 8KB, originally sent as 50 tiny packets, but it can be retransmitted as ~6 QUIC packets. We have literal seconds to retransmit 6 packets to avoid any user impact.
And if we manage to accomplish this herculean task: all the context arrives in time!
The model no longer has to guess. It no longer has to be trained on silence or distortion either. This is a pure user experience win.
Not Just Mics
Guess what? WebRTC doesn’t just suck for STT, it also sucks for TTS.
Fun Fact: WebRTC renders audio (and video) based on when it arrives, not when it is supposed to be rendered. Every other protocol uses timestamps, but Mr. WebRTC barely looks at them, because accuracy is a non-goal. Sure, it’ll nudge audio and video into sync by a few milliseconds, but good luck sending the video 500ms after the audio.
This is a huge problem for voice AI. TTS is generated faster than real-time, stamping each packet with a future timestamp. But in order to play back audio at the correct time with WebRTC… the agent needs to sleep before transmitting each packet.
And if there’s any packet loss, our TTS is lost, will never be retransmitted, tokens burned, yada yada.
If only there was some way to signal when to render each audio packet. A stamp of sorts.
Random Access Memory
Welcome back to the future Marty. We faster than real-time now.
RAM has this amazing property of being stupidly expensive. And being able to store stuff locally. You know, like audio that needs to be played over the speakers.
We put a timestamp on each audio frame and use that to determine when to play it out of RAM. Absurd, I know.
It’s how the Youtubes keeps playing back video even when you lose network connectivity. MoQ does the same thing but for voice AI. Your sick baking recipe won’t be subject to surprise congestion.
And don’t you fret, 2 minutes of audio is only 1MB. You’re not going to have to take out a loan to buy another RAM stick.
Disclaimer: this behavior is not IETF standardized. It’s something only my moq.dev clients (and thus Pipecat) support. Be my guest if you want to argue with Cisco and get it into the official standards.
Enter the Antagonist
Then why is OpenAI using WebRTC?
WebRTC is the state of the art for real-time, conversational audio.
It’s available in every browser via libwebrtc, a C++ monolith maintained by Google.
It’s so complicated and sophisticated that Safari and Firefox use libwebrtc too, rather than vibe code their own like everything else.
The problem is that WebRTC is the Google Meet client. It is designed specifically for Google’s conferencing product, not their voice AI product (they use WebSocket), and certainly not your product.
quite the anti-competitive ruse tbh. Google can ship product updates without consulting the other browser vendors. No other conferencing app can do this on the web.
Fun Fact: This is why every other conferencing app recommends a native client. Otherwise, they can only reach parity with Google Meet at best. Native apps can do whatever they want over UDP instead.
Fix It Fix It Fix It
So that’s why your hyper deluxe ChatGPT™ voice AI model, after billions invested, has the audacity to ask: can you repeat that?
I could dump on WebRTC for days, but I want to be positive for a change. Here’s how to fix it.
First off, I need to acknowledge what WebRTC does have:
- NetEQ is amazing. It changes audio playback speed based on jitter. But not packet loss.
- Audio retransmissions can now be enabled via SDP munging (disgusting). But the NetEQ jitter buffer won’t wait for them.
- The playout-delay RTP extension is perfect for voice AI. But it’s video only.
To fix WebRTC, we need to petition Google to:
- Implement playout-delay for audio.
- Allow the jitter buffer to grow, both in the past and into the future (for TTS).
- Render audio based on timestamps not vibes.
- IDK some RTP extension to bump the track generation (for interruptions).
And of course, petition the wider WebRTC ecosystem to do the same.
Gatekept
The main problem with WebRTC will remain: Google is the gatekeeper.
Your Claude friend can’t just fork libwebrtc and fix these issues.
Google is required for web support, at least until Theo spends $420k to rewrite Chromium in Rust.
I think it’s amazing that playout-delay was merged 10 years ago and audio still doesn’t have it. Higher latency/quality playback has never been a priority for WebRTC, since Google Meet is the only product that matters.
Fun Fact: This is why I ended up creating MoQ. We tried using WebRTC at Twitch but the real-time-or-else made for a poor user experience. I am but a humble software engineer, and despite trying, we failed to petition Google.
But OpenAI has enough sway to fix WebRTC. One long-deserved improvement is WARP (not that WARP), which was hot on the heels of my last blog post. Keep at it Justin, or join the Dark Side with me.
Enter The Protagonist
In my humble and handsome opinion, it’s time to invest in a better transport. Take a few of the M’s from the B’s and T’s; nobody will notice.
A voice agent should never ask the user to retransmit a prompt.
A voice agent should instead ask the transport to retransmit a prompt.
Spoiler alert: Media over QUIC is that better transport btw.
Pipecat now supports MoQ! A huge thank you to Vanessa and Claude Code for putting in the work and putting up with my constant “improvements”.
Here’s a crude demo with my credit card deets attached. please don’t milk me dry.
Note that I’ve only spent like a day of work prompting on this.
It took me significantly longer to write this damn blog post.
Don’t judge too harshly pls.
And yes, it sometimes says “can you repeat that?” which is hilariously ironic. The first/last hop is MoQ, but I don’t control the rest of the pipeline. If Deepgram, OpenAI, or Cartesia drop ur packets then there’s nothing I can do about it.
Interruptions
We’re not done yet. I wanted to shill the MoQ in the middle of the blog and use the rest…
Sometimes the AI is monologuing and you need to tell it to STFU. It’s pretty easy to do with WebRTC because of the sleep before sending each packet. But with MoQ, we need some signal to tell the player to abandon the playout buffer.
Here’s the naive approach without a signal:
notdo this on my first implementation.
My solution for this is deviously clever. So clever.
For MoQ, we’ve prioritized the ability to add/remove tracks dynamically. Most media protocols have fixed tracks and it’s a pain in the butt: HLS, DASH, RTMP, WebRTC, etc. You can’t add 1080p, or switch codecs, after a broadcast is live.
My super clever idea is to reuse this functionality for interruptions. Just make a new audio track (and remove the old one) as the STFU Signal™.
This works on a generic MoQ player. We automatically switch tracks, using timestamps to keep synchronization.
ez
Butt-to-Butt
Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. You didn’t mention speech-to-speech?
Look, Dunning-Kruger is the only reason the previous blog post exists. I didn’t know speech-to-speech existed until the comment section. What can I say but ur welcome.
DISCLAIMER: I still haven’t done any research on the state of voice AI.
I give you full permission to tweet @kixelated ur stupid.
The idea behind speech-to-speech is to cut out the text middleman. The disjoint STT -> LLM -> TTS pipelines get smashed together, reducing latency while preserving verbal context. OpenAI is the pioneer in this space and they deserve mad props.
So this vindicates WebRTC right? The speech-to-speech latency can be low enough to justify dropping packets?
Not so fast literary strawman. There’s a fundamental trade-off between latency and quality.
Latency Budgets
The more time you have to work on something, the better the result.
Good things take time, like Fable changing a single line in README.md because I’m too poor to pay 3.5x for ultrafast.
Networks are the same. The more time you have to transmit something, the better the quality. It’s why retransmits exist in the first place.
Unless you’re doing broadcast TV, which still uses MPEG-TS and still results in glitchy messes. Seriously wtf guys, TV is no longer over the air, and we don’t need 188 byte packets any longer.
Anyway, the amount of time a user is willing to wait for something is a product decision. Put on your big boye pants, it’s time to be a PM. Do users want something fast and lossy, or slow and reliable?
Why not both?
That’s the idea behind speech-to-speech. Do a low-latency STS pass for easy prompts and to generate filler noise.
Human: What is le capital of France?
ChatGPT: One second, let me look that up.
Boom, even that useless “I’m thinking” response makes the human feel good chemicals. But more importantly for us anti-PMs, it buys us enough time to start a slower pass.
I don’t work at a frontier lab so this is all speculation, but I imagine STT->LLM->TTS is still used for these slower passes. A STS model with Astra/Fable quality is absolutely ideal… but probably not worth the investment.
Either way, doesn’t matter if it’s STS or STT->LLM->TTS. The only thing that matters is the latency budget.
MoQ do Both
One of the core problems we’re trying to fix with MoQ is the whole “one transport per latency” issue in the industry. It’s face-palmingly common to use different protocols based on the latency budget.
For example, an all-hands presentation where the speakers use Zoom, while everybody else watches via HLS and can’t participate.
Fuck that noise, MoQ supports multiple latency targets with a single connection. In the case of voice AI:
- real-time latency for rapid replies (STS).
- loss-less quality for slow replies (STT->LLM->TTS).
How? Every MoQ subscription includes how long the subscriber is willing to wait.
Your real-time model can have a maximum latency of 500ms while your more accurate model might have a maximum latency of 5s. Both get coalesced into a single upstream subscription which can fanout.
And note that this is the maximum latency. The latency is 0 except during terrible network conditions, and eventually we give up. This is the core difference between MoQ and TCP/WebSocket for Voice AI.
Your transport latency should be aligned with your product latency budget.
It’s Simple: Predict the Future
One more strawman to beat into the dirt.
Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. WebRTC doesn’t care about packet loss because it uses FEC.
M8 go read my previous blog posts: never use datagrams and forward error correction. This is like my dumber one hot take.
WebRTC (and Opus) include Forward Error Correction to help mask packet loss. The idea is to stuff a crappier, lower bitrate copy of the previous audio frame into the next packet.
But only a single last packet. It can’t even handle two lost packets in a row, let alone a full network blip.
This is fine for WebRTC because it doesn’t give a shit about audio older than 30ms. But it’s not fine for voice AI or really anything on the internet. Packet loss due to congestion is bursty, not random.
A common “fix” is to spread these copies over time, so you can handle X lost packets in a row. See Opus 1.5. All of this extra data has a real cost, and if you don’t know what you’re doing (and you don’t), then you will aggravate bufferbloat.
In my humble (and attractive) opinion, FEC is best for huge RTTs, like transmitting to le moon.
In <current year>, we instead use CDNs to shrink the lossy first/last mile which makes retransmissions OP.
Why send more bytes spread over 400ms, instead of retransmitting in 40ms?
But if a WebRTC warrior insists, QUIC libraries can retransmit stream data as many times as they want. Basically RED but based on byte offsets, not packets, and fully transparent to the receiver. That’s a free idea btw.

PostgreSQL 19 Released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
14:11:37 UTC
23:11:37 KST

November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today announced the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.
Mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and
PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and
development for these workloads at scale. This release introduces the
REPACK (CONCURRENTLY)
command so users can optimize tables for their current workload without
disruption to ongoing operations. PostgreSQL 19 gives users better control over
plan stability and query performance with the new pg_plan_advice
extension. Developers will find many delightful features in this release, from
support for "read-your-writes" consistency on standbys to "get or create"
behavior that saves a network round trip.
"For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team. "PostgreSQL 19 continues that commitment to reliability, giving users new ways to manage their workloads without disruption and to build applications that span multiple systems."
PostgreSQL, an innovative data management system known for its reliability, robustness, and extensibility, benefits from 30 years of open source development from a global developer community and has become the preferred open source relational database for organizations of all sizes.
Tables that receive many updates and deletes can build up unused space, known as
"bloat," which can also significantly impact query performance. The
VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands were previously used to handle this, but
had tradeoffs, including preventing access to the table until the cleanup
finished. PostgreSQL 19 introduces the REPACK
command, which reclaims this space and can reorder a table's data to match an
index, and with REPACK (CONCURRENTLY), can do so without blocking reads or
writes. REPACK replaces the VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands, both of
which remain available for compatibility.
The PostgreSQL query planner usually picks an efficient plan for each query, but
the plan can change as your data changes, and sometimes the new plan is slower.
PostgreSQL 19 adds the pg_plan_advice
extension, which allows stabilization of plan choices and the ability to
experiment with different plans using the "plan advice" mini-language. The companion
pg_stash_advice
extension stores advice and automatically applies it to queries based on their
query identifier, so you can fix a slow plan without changing your application.
PostgreSQL 19 also helps autovacuum
keep up on busy systems. Autovacuum can now vacuum indexes using parallel
workers, controlled by the new
autovacuum_max_parallel_workers
setting, and uses a new scoring system
to decide which tables to process first. Queries that read a table can now
automatically mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map during execution,
reducing the work that future vacuums need to do. Additionally,
vacuumdb --analyze-only
now analyzes partitioned tables when no tables are specified.
This release adds new views for monitoring workloads, including
pg_stat_lock
for per-lock-type statistics, pg_stat_recovery
for recovery status, and pg_stat_autovacuum_scores
to show how autovacuum prioritizes tables. The new IO option for
EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the
matching auto_explain
setting report asynchronous I/O activity. PostgreSQL 19 also reports the amount
of WAL written for full-page images in pg_stat_wal,
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL), and in vacuum and analyze log events.
Previously, PostgreSQL often required users to restart their server to enable
logical replication,
which could be disruptive in production workloads. PostgreSQL 19 simplifies
logical replication initialization by automatically raising the effective WAL
level to logical when you create the first logical replication slot. You can
see the WAL level in use with the new effective_wal_level setting.
PostgreSQL 19 also adds logical replication of
sequence values,
which you can publish using FOR ALL SEQUENCES with
CREATE PUBLICATION.
CREATE PUBLICATION also adds an EXCEPT clause to exclude tables when
publishing FOR ALL TABLES, and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION
can now get its connection settings from a foreign server, such as one defined
with postgres_fdw,
using the SERVER clause. Additionally, the new
retain_dead_tuples
subscription option lets PostgreSQL detect updates that conflict with a
concurrent delete, and these conflicts are counted in
pg_stat_subscription_stats.
For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds
"read-your-writes" consistency with the new
WAIT FOR LSN command. A
session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has
replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific
log sequence number (LSN)
before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the
primary.
PostgreSQL 19 also improves queries on foreign tables. With the new
import_stats option,
postgres_fdw can
import table statistics from the remote server when you run ANALYZE, instead
of sampling rows from the remote table, which helps the query planner choose
better plans.
PostgreSQL 19 adds INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT,
which lets the RETURNING clause return existing rows that conflict with an
insert, simplifying the common "get or create" pattern.
COPY can now output data
as JSON, including as a single JSON array, and the
SQL/JSON path language
adds string methods such as lower(), upper(), replace(), split_part(),
and btrim(). Additionally, the lead(), lag(), first_value(),
last_value(), and nth_value() window functions
can now skip NULL values using IGNORE NULLS. The random() function can now also generate random dates
and timestamps within a range.
This release also makes many workloads faster without changes to your
application. PostgreSQL 19 improves the performance of foreign key checks, which
in testing made bulk inserts nearly 2x faster, and adds more query planner
optimizations, such as converting NOT IN clauses to more efficient anti-joins
when NULL values are not present, and performing
eager aggregation
before joins to reduce the number of rows to process. PostgreSQL 19 also builds
on the asynchronous I/O
subsystem added in PostgreSQL 18. When io_method is set to worker (the
default), PostgreSQL now automatically adjusts the number of I/O workers between
the new io_min_workers
and io_max_workers
settings, which replace the io_workers setting. There are also scalability
improvements when using LISTEN
and NOTIFY to
exchange notifications in multi-channel workloads.
Finally, the new password_expiration_warning_threshold
setting warns users when their password is about to expire.
PostgreSQL 19 adds server-side support for
Server Name Indication (SNI),
letting a single PostgreSQL server present a different TLS certificate based on
the hostname a client connects to. You can map hostnames to their certificates
and keys in the new pg_hosts.conf
file. PostgreSQL 19 also now issues a warning after a successful md5 password
authentication, which you can turn off with the
md5_password_warnings
setting. md5 password authentication was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and will
be removed in a future release. If you require password-based authentication,
use SCRAM authentication.
This release also removes support for RADIUS authentication.
Just-in-time compilation (JIT) is
now disabled by default, as the cost estimates PostgreSQL used to decide when to
use it proved unreliable. If you run many large analytical queries, you may want
to enable JIT. When PostgreSQL is built with LZ4 support, the default
TOAST compression
method is now lz4.
Many other new features and improvements have been added to PostgreSQL 19 that may also be helpful for your use cases. Please see the release notes for a complete list of new and changed features.
PostgreSQL is the world's most advanced open source database, with a global community of thousands of users, contributors, companies and organizations. Since its beginnings at the University of California, Berkeley over 40 years ago, PostgreSQL has continued with an unmatched pace of development. PostgreSQL's mature feature set not only matches top proprietary database systems, but exceeds them in advanced database features, extensibility, security, and stability.

Added new stream errors API including new StreamException, StreamError classes, StreamErrorStore, StreamErrorMode, StreamErrorCode enums, stream_last_errors() and stream_clear_errors() functions, error_mode, error_store and error_handler stream context options and extending some stream functions with context param.

MBString:
mb_detect_encoding is better able to identify the correct encoding for Turkish text.
mb_detect_encoding's "non-strict" mode now behaves as described in the documentation. Previously, it would return false if the same byte (for example, the first byte) of the input string was invalid in all candidate encodings. More generally, it would eliminate candidate encodings from consideration when an invalid byte was seen, and if the same input byte eliminated all remaining encodings still under consideration, it would return false. On the other hand, if all candidate encodings but one were eliminated from consideration, it would return the last remaining one without regard for how many encoding errors might be encountered later in the string. This is different from the behavior described in the documentation, which says: "If strict is set to false, the closest matching encoding will be returned." (Alex Dowad)
mb_strtolower, mb_strtotitle, and mb_convert_case implement conditional casing rules for the Greek letter sigma. For mb_convert_case, conditional casing only applies to MB_CASE_LOWER and MB_CASE_TITLE modes, not to MB_CASE_LOWER_SIMPLE and MB_CASE_TITLE_SIMPLE.
mb_detect_encoding is better able to identify UTF-8 and UTF-16 strings with a byte-order mark.
mb_decode_mimeheader interprets underscores in QPrint-encoded MIME encoded words as required by RFC 2047; they are converted to spaces. Underscores must be encoded as "=5F" in such MIME encoded words.
mb_encode_mimeheader no longer drops NUL (zero) bytes when QPrint-encoding the input string. This previously caused strings in certain text encodings, especially UTF-16 and UTF-32, to be corrupted by mb_encode_mimeheader.
Implement mb_str_pad() RFC.

mb_detect_encoding's "non-strict" mode now behaves as described in the documentation. Previously, it would return false if the same byte (for example, the first byte) of the input string was invalid in all candidate encodings. More generally, it would eliminate candidate encodings from consideration when an invalid byte was seen, and if the same input byte eliminated all remaining encodings still under consideration, it would return false. On the other hand, if all candidate encodings but one were eliminated from consideration, it would return the last remaining one without regard for how many encoding errors might be encountered later in the string. This is different from the behavior described in the documentation, which says: "If strict is set to false, the closest matching encoding will be returned." (Alex Dowad)
mb_strtolower, mb_strtotitle, and mb_convert_case implement conditional casing rules for the Greek letter sigma. For mb_convert_case, conditional casing only applies to MB_CASE_LOWER and MB_CASE_TITLE modes, not to MB_CASE_LOWER_SIMPLE and MB_CASE_TITLE_SIMPLE.
mb_detect_encoding is better able to identify UTF-8 and UTF-16 strings with a byte-order mark.
mb_decode_mimeheader interprets underscores in QPrint-encoded MIME encoded words as required by RFC 2047; they are converted to spaces. Underscores must be encoded as "=5F" in such MIME encoded words.
mb_encode_mimeheader no longer drops NUL (zero) bytes when QPrint-encoding the input string. This previously caused strings in certain text encodings, especially UTF-16 and UTF-32, to be corrupted by mb_encode_mimeheader.

The End of the Beginning of the End for Journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-19
14:00:39 UTC
23:00:39 KST

The End of the Beginning of the End for Journalism
Posted on November 19, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 24 Comments
My first job out of college was for a McClatchy newspaper, the Fresno Bee, and it’s safe to say that this newspaper was hit pretty hard by the decline of local journalism; when I visited it ten years ago on a trip to California, not much of the staff was left and what was there was inhabiting a corner of a building formerly bustling with activity. I can’t imagine how this “Pivot to AI” is going to help anyone still at that paper, or any paper in the McClatchy chain, or any of the people who still subscribe and rely on these papers. “AI” creates junk content and it can’t do journalism. It can’t report from an event. It can’t cultivate sources. It can’t interview people. All it can do is repack what’s already been said by others, with increasing levels of hallucination.
Whatever McClatchy is going to be now, it’s not going to be what it was, and what it should be for the communities it purports to serve. If you’re a McClatchy subscriber, you might want to start looking elsewhere for news about where you live.
(If you’re in Fresno or the Central Valley, btw, here’s a site by humans to support.)
— jS
